newsitem.title: CANADA: BASEBALL-TORONTO TRADES OLERUD TO METS.
newsitem.headline: BASEBALL-TORONTO TRADES OLERUD TO METS.

text.p: After spending freely to attract players, the Toronto Blue Jays paid a bundle to get rid of one Friday, dealing John Olerud to the New York Mets and agreeing to pay $5 million of his 1997 salary.
In return for first baseman Olerud, the 1993 American League batting champion whose production has declined in each season since, the Mets sent Toronto unproven right-handed starter Robert Person.

The sweet-swinging Olerud, whose salary next season is $6.5 million, batted .363 and flirted with the magical .400 mark for much of the year. Last season, the 28-year-old batted .274 with 18 home runs and 61 runs batted in.
"It's a good time to get a player, in the last year of his contract," New York general manager Joe McIlvaine said in a conference call. "He's got a lot to play for."
The move is the latest in a hectic off-season for the Jays, determined to be contenders once again.

Since finishing fourth in their division last season, the 1992 and '93 World Series champions have signed free-agent pitcher Roger Clemens to a $25-million deal, picked up catcher Benito Santiago and traded for second baseman Carlos Garcia, outfielder Orlando Merced and left-handed pitcher Dan Plesac.
Moving Olerud dumps $1.5 million off the payroll and opens up room in the Blue Jays' lineup.
Manager Cito Gaston will now be able to use Joe Carter and Carlos Delgado as first basemen and designated hitters, creating an outfield spot for Merced.

The Mets have been looking for a first baseman to replace Rico Brogna, who was traded to the Philadelphia Phillies last month. The trade left Butch Huskey, who struggled in the field last season, at first base.
Since his sensational 1993 season, the 28-year-old Olerud hit .297 in 1994 and .291 in 1995 before falling another 17 points last season.
The hard-throwing Person, 27, was 4-5 with a 4.52 ERA in 27 games and 13 starts last season. He ended the season with eight starts in his final 10 outings.
"They got a real fine arm and a guy with only 155 days of major-league service time so he's someone they can hang on to for a long time," said McIlvaine.
